label: thmA:alternatives
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmA:alternatives}
  Let $X$ be a Haar system space with the Fatou property and non-trivial Boyd indices, and let $Y = X^0$.
  Then one of the following exclusive alternatives holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),topsep=5pt]
    \item\label{thmA:alternatives:a} There exists a strictly increasing transfinite sequence of countable ordinals $(\alpha_\xi)_{\xi< \omega_1}$ such that the spaces $R_{\alpha_\xi}^{Y}$, $\xi < \omega_1$, are pairwise non-isomorphic.
    \item\label{thmA:alternatives:b} For every ordinal $\omega \le \alpha < \omega_1$, the space $R_\alpha^{Y}$ is isomorphic to $Y$.
  \end{enumerate}

title: Notation
body_md:
\label{measure theory notation}
For a measurable subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}$, we denote by $|A|$ its Lebesgue measure. We denote by $L_0$ the space of equivalence classes of scalar-valued measurable functions on the unit interval. Equipped with convergence in measure, $L_0$ is a Polish topological vector space, induced, e.g., by the metric $d(f,g) = \|(f-g)(1+|f-g|)^{-1}\|_1$. We denote $L_1 = \{f\in L_0:\;\int|f|dx<\infty\}$ and $L_1^0 = \{f\in L_1: \int f dx = 0\}$. For $f\in L_0$, the distribution of $f$ is the probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathrm{dist}(f)(A) = |[f\in A]|$. For a countably indexed collection $(f_i)_{i\in I}$ in $L_0$, its joint distribution is the probability measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^I)$ given by $\mathrm{dist}((f_i)_{i\in I})(A) = |[(f_i)_{i\in I}\in A]|$. For a vector subspace $W$ of $L_0$, a linear map $T:W\to L_0$ is called a distributional embedding if, for every $f\in W$, $\mathrm{dist}(Tf) = \mathrm{dist}(f)$. Every distributional embedding $T\colon W \to L_0$ extends uniquely to a distributional embedding defined on the closure of~$W$ with respect to convergence in measure (since convergence in measure implies convergence in distribution). For such a map, letting $Z = T(W)$, we then write $Z\equiv^\mathrm{dist} W$ and say that $T$ is a distributional isomorphism onto $Z$. Two commonly indexed countable collections $(f_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(g_i)_{i\in I}$ in $L_0$ are called distributionally equivalent if they have the same joint distribution. By a standard probability theory fact based on the multivariable characteristic function, the previous statement is equivalent to the map $f_i\mapsto g_i$ extending to a distributional embedding from $\langle\{f_i:i\in I\}\rangle$ onto $\langle\{g_i:i\in I\}\rangle$.

body_md:
\label{dyadic haar rademacher notation}
We establish the notation for dyadic intervals, the Haar system, and the Rademacher sequence.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),]

\item For $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, we let
\begin{gather*}
\mathcal{D}^n = \Big\{\Big[\frac{i-1}{2^n},\frac{i}{2^n}\Big):1\leq i\leq 2^n\Big\},\quad \mathcal{D}_n = \cup_{k=0}^n\mathcal{D}^k,\quad \text{and}\quad \mathcal{D} = \cup_{k=0}^\infty\mathcal{D}^k.
\end{gather*}
We enumerate $\mathcal{D}$ according to the lexicographical order, defined by declaring $I<J$ whenever $|I|>|J|$, or $|I|=|J|$ and $\sup(I)\le \inf(J)$.
For any collection $\mathcal{B}$ of dyadic intervals, we write $\mathcal{B}^{*} = \cup_{I\in \mathcal{B}}I$.
        
\item For $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and $I = [(i-1)/2^n,i/2^n)\in\mathcal{D}^n$ we denote the left and right half of $I$ as follows:
\[I^+ = \Big[\frac{2i-2}{2^{n+1}},\frac{2i-1}{2^{n+1}}\Big)\text{ and } I^- = \Big[\frac{2i-1}{2^{n+1}},\frac{2i}{2^{n+1}}\Big).\]
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $I\in\mathcal{D}^n$ we denote by $\pi(I)$ the unique member of $\mathcal{D}^{n-1}$ such that $I = \pi(I)^+$ or $\pi(I)^-$. In the former case, we define $\varepsilon(I) = 1$ and in the latter $\varepsilon(I) = -1$.

\item The standard Haar system $(h_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}}$ is defined as follows: for $I\in\mathcal{D}$, let
\[h_I = \chi_{I^+} - \chi_{I^{-}}.\]

\item The standard Rademacher sequence $(r_n)_{n=0}^\infty$ is defined by letting, for $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,
\[r_n = \sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^n}h_I.\]

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[resume,label=(\alph*),]

\[Y_F = \big\{f\in L_1^0 : f \text{ is } \sigma_F\text{-measurable}\big\}.\]

\[\mathbb{E}_F \colon L_1^0 \to Y_F\]
for the conditional expectation operator with respect to $\sigma_F$.

In the special case where $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $F=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$, we write $\sigma_n$, $Y_n$, and $\mathbb{E}_n$ for the corresponding objects.

\item\label{notation of subsequences of the levels b} We denote by $J_F:Y_n\to Y_F$ the unique distributional embedding given by extending the map $r_i \mapsto r_{k_i}$, $0\leq i\leq n$ (which exists by \Cref{distroembedding extension}). We then define the distributional copy of the Haar system $(b_I^F)_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}$ by letting, for $I\in\mathcal{D}_n$,
\[b^F_I = J_Fh_I.\]
\end{enumerate}
The above are also defined for an infinite $F$ in the obvious way.

label: comparing haar system to ri
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{comparing haar system to ri}
Haar system spaces whose norm is not equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ provide a concise framework for separable rearrangement invariant spaces (over the unit interval), with the Haar system highlighted as the main underlying structure. While there is no universally accepted definition of this class, a minimal formulation is to define a rearrangement invariant space as an order ideal $X$ in $L_0$ containing $\chi_{[0,1)}$, equipped with a complete norm $\|\cdot\|_X$ such that $\|\chi_{[0,1)}\|_X = 1$ and whenever $f\in X$ and $g\in L_0$ has the same distribution as $f$, it follows that $g\in X$ and $\|g\|_X=\|f\|_X$ (see, e.g., \cite{rodin:semyonov:1975}). Henceforth, this is what we will mean by a rearrangement-invariant space. Given a Haar system space $X$, the identity map $id:(\langle\{\chi_I:I\in\mathcal{D}\}\rangle,\|\cdot\|_X)\to L_1\subset L_0$ extends to a continuous linear injection on $X$ (see, e.g., \cite[the introduction of Section 2.4]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}). We may thus naturally identify $X$ with a subspace of $L_0$. If $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$, the image of $X$ in $L_0$ is a separable rearrangement invariant space (see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 2.4.3]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}). Conversely, every separable rearrangement invariant space admits $(\chi_{[0,1)})\cup(h_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}}$ as a basis, and therefore coincides with a Haar system space whose norm is not equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ (see \cite[Proposition~2.c.1]{lindenstrauss:tzafriri:1979:partII} or the proof of~\cite[Chapter~1, Theorem~5.5]{bennett:sharpley:1988}).

The Fatou property, which is commonly included in the definition of rearrangement invariant spaces (see \Cref{Fatou property definition}), is not included in \Cref{haar system space} because a large part of the theory of Haar system spaces can be developed without it (see, e.g., \cite{lechner:motakis:mueller:schlumprecht:2022}, \cite{lechner:speckhofer:2025}, \cite{speckhofer:2025}, and \cite{MR5094444}).
Haar system spaces with $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$ coincide with \emph{minimal} rearrangement-invariant function spaces over~$[0,1]$ in the terminology of~\cite{lindenstrauss:tzafriri:1979:partII} (see \Cref{rem:lindenstrauss-tzafriri}).
On the other hand, Haar system spaces with $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$ that have the Fatou property are \emph{maximal} rearrangement-invariant in the sense of~\cite{lindenstrauss:tzafriri:1979:partII}.
We note, purely for context, that a Haar system space $X$ satisfies the Fatou property if and only if it does not contain an isomorphic copy of the Banach space $c_0$.

label: pro:HS-1d
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pro:HS-1d}
  Let $X$ be a Haar system space. Then the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item\label{pro:HS-1d:i} For every $f\in H:= \langle \{ \chi_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \} \rangle$, we have
          $\|f\|_{L_1}\leq \|f\|_X\leq \|f\|_{L_\infty}$.
    \item\label{pro:HS-1d:v} For all $f,g\in H$ with $|f|\leq |g|$, we have $\|f\|_X \leq \|g\|_X$.
    \item\label{pro:HS-1d:ii} The Haar system $(\chi_{[0,1)})\cup (h_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$, in the usual linear
          order, is a monotone Schauder basis of~$X$.
    \item \label{pro:HS-1d:iii} $H$ naturally coincides with a subspace of $X^{*}$ (where $f\in H$ acts on $g\in H$ by $\langle f,g \rangle = \int fg$), and its closure in $X^{*}$ is also a Haar system space.
  \end{enumerate}

label: rem:lindenstrauss-tzafriri
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:lindenstrauss-tzafriri}
  The above properties allow us to show that the Haar system spaces $X$ with $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$ coincide with the separable \emph{minimal} rearrangement-invariant function spaces on~$[0,1]$, as defined in~\cite[Definition~2.a.1]{lindenstrauss:tzafriri:1979:partII}. Indeed, if $X$ is a Haar system space with $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$, then by \cite[Theorem~2.4.3]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}, $X$ is a K\"othe function space. It follows from \cite[Theorem~2.4.8 and Remark~2.4.9]{speckhofer:2025:thesis} that condition~(i) of \cite[Definition~2.a.1]{lindenstrauss:tzafriri:1979:partII} holds (i.e., invariance of~$X$ and its norm under automorphisms of the unit interval). Condition~(ii) holds because the Haar system is a monotone Schauder basis of~$X$, so its linear span in $X^{*}$ is norming and $X$ is the closed span of simple integrable functions in its K\"othe bidual~$X''$ (note that by \cite[Proposition 2.4.2]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}, $L_{\infty}\subset X$). Condition~(iii) follows from the discussion in \Cref{comparing haar system to ri}, \cite[Proposition 2.4.2]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}, and \Cref{pro:HS-1d}~\ref{pro:HS-1d:i}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $f\in L_1^0$, $\|f\|_1\lesssim \|S(f)\|_1$ (see \cite{davis:1970} or \cite[Theorem 8.7]{AdamOse:2012}) and, for every $g\in X$, $\|g\|_1\le \|g\|_X$ (see, e.g., \cite[Proposition 2.3.1]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}). Consequently, for every $f\in \langle\{h_I:I\in\mathcal{D}\}\rangle$, $\|f\|_1\lesssim \|S(f)\|_X$, which implies boundedness of $id$. Since $id$ maps the Haar system onto itself, and this is a Schauder basis for both $L_1^0$ and $H_X$, the extension of $id$ is injective. To obtain \eqref{Hardy space included}, observe that for every $f\in H_X$ and $m,n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,
$\|S(\mathbb{E}_m f)-S(\mathbb{E}_n f)\|_X \le \|S(\mathbb{E}_n f-\mathbb{E}_m f)\|_X$.
Thus $(S(\mathbb{E}_n f))$ is Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_X$, and therefore its pointwise limit $S(f)$ belongs to $X$. The same argument yields $\|f\|_{H_X}=\|S(f)\|_X$. If, in addition, $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and $f\in L_1^0$ satisfies $S(f)\in X$, then for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we have $S(\mathbb{E}_{(n,\infty)}f)\in X$, and this sequence decreases pointwise to zero. By \cite[Proposition 2.4.7]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}, it follows that $\|S(\mathbb{E}_{(n,\infty)}f)\|_X\to 0$. Hence $(\mathbb{E}_{n}f)_{n=0}^\infty$ is Cauchy in $H_X$, and therefore $f\in H_X$.

title: Definition

\[\mathrm{dist}\big(S(Jf)\big) = \mathrm{dist}(Sf).\]
Denoting $W = J(Z)$, we then write $Z\equiv^{S\text{-dist}}W$ and say that $J$ is a square function-distributional isomorphism onto $Z$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{standard square function distributional isomorphism}
Let $F = \{k_0,\ldots, k_n\}$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{N}_0$. Then $J_F:Y_n\to Y_F$ is a square function-distributional embedding. If $F$ is infinite, the same is true for $J_F:L_1^0\to Y_F$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F = \{k_0,\ldots, k_n\}$ and $\tilde J_F:L_0(\sigma(Y_n)) = \langle \chi_{[0,1)}\rangle+Y_n\to L_0$ denote the extension of $J_F$ defined in \Cref{distroembedding extension}. Then, for $f = \sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}a_Ih_I\in Y_n$,
\begin{align*}
S(J_Ff) &= S\Big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}a_Ib^F_I\Big) = \Big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}a_I^2\chi_{\mathrm{supp}(b_I^F)}\Big)^{1/2} = \Big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}a_I^2\tilde J_F\chi_{\mathrm{supp}(h_I)}\Big)^{1/2}\\
        &=\tilde J_F\Big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}_n}a_I^2\chi_{\mathrm{supp}(h_I)}\Big)^{1/2}\quad \text{(because $\tilde J_F$ is a homomorphism)}\\
  &= \tilde J_F\big(Sf\big).
\end{align*}
This yields $\mathrm{dist}\big(S(J_Ff)\big) = \mathrm{dist}(S(f))$.

The statement about infinite $F$ follows from the continuity of $S:L_1^0\to L_0$ and $f = \lim_n\mathbb{E}_nf$ in $L_1^0$.

\label{def augmented disjoint sum}
For two subspaces $Z$, $W$ of $L_0$ we define their disjoint sum as
\[(Z\oplus W)_{\mathrm{disj}} = T_{[0,1/2)}(Z)+T_{[1/2,1)}(W).\]
If $Z,W\subset L_1^0$, then $h_{[0,1)}\notin(Z\oplus W)_{\mathrm{disj}}$, and we define their augmented disjoint sum as
\[(Z\oplus W)_{\mathrm{disj}}^+ = \langle\{ h_{[0,1)}\}\rangle + (Z\oplus W)_{\mathrm{disj}},\]

label: why augment
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{why augment}
In \cite{bourgain:rosenthal:schechtman:1981}, Bourgain-Rosenthal-Schechtman spaces are constructed using disjoint sums together with independent sums (formulated on different underlying measure spaces). In that setting, the spaces always contain the constant function and therefore are not subspaces of $L_1^0$. When working inside $L_1^0$, to preserve the distributional properties of the construction, disjoint sums must be replaced with  their augmented counterparts, since for any $Z,W\subset L_1$ containing the constant function,
\[(Z\oplus W)_{\mathrm{disj}}\cap L_1^0=\big((Z\cap L_1^0)\oplus (W\cap L_1^0)\big)_{\mathrm{disj}}^+.\]
The outcome of this adjustment is that if we denote by $R_\alpha^p$ a Bourgain-Rosenthal-Schechtman space constructed via the iteration in \cite{bourgain:rosenthal:schechtman:1981} (up to identifications of the underlying measure spaces) and by $R_\alpha^Y$, where $Y = L_p^0$, the corresponding space constructed in this paper, then $R_\alpha^p\cap L_1^0 = R_\alpha^Y$ (see \Cref{same spaces sans constant}).

Independent sums do not need to be adjusted to achieve $R_\alpha\cap L_1^0 = R_\alpha^0$.

\label{dfn:independence}
\label{independence}~
Let $(X_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of subspaces of $L_1^0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item We call $(X_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ independent if the $\sigma$-algebras $\sigma(X_n)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, are independent.

\item\label{square function-independence} We call $(X_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ square function-independent if, for every eventually zero sequence $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\in\prod_{n=1}^\infty X_n$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

\item\label{square function-independence a} $(Sf_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{ is independent and }$

\item\label{square function-independence b} $S\big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\big) = \Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty S^2(f_n)\Big)^{1/2}.$

\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{canonical properties of independent sums}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space and $Y = X^0$
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item\label{canonical properties of independent sums a} The choice of operators in \Cref{def independent sum} does not matter, up to distributional isomorphism: if $J_n'$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, is another such sequence then
\[\big[\big(J_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty\big]\equiv^\mathrm{dist}\big[\big(J'_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty\big].\]

\item\label{canonical properties of independent sums b} If $(Z_n)_{n=1}^\infty$, $(Z_n')_{n=1}^\infty$ are subspaces of $Y$ such that, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $Z_n\equiv^\mathrm{dist} Z_n'$, then
\[\big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty Z_n\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}\equiv^\mathrm{dist} \big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty Z_n'\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}.\]

\item\label{canonical properties of independent sums c} If $(Z_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ are subspaces of $Y$ and $\pi\colon \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}$ is a bijection, then
\[\big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty Z_n\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}\equiv^\mathrm{dist} \big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty Z_{\pi(n)}\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}.\]

\item\label{canonical properties of independent sums d} If $(Z_m^n)_{m,n=1}^\infty$ are subspaces of $Y$, then
\[\Big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty\big(\oplus_{m=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}\Big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}\equiv^\mathrm{dist} \big(\oplus_{m,n=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}},\]
where the enumeration of the sum on the right-hand side does not matter.

\end{enumerate}
If  instead $Y = H_X$, the above statements remain valid, replacing ``distributional isomorphism'' with ``square function-distributional isomorphism'' and ``$\equiv^\mathrm{dist}$'' with ``$\equiv^{S\text{-dist}}$''.

title: Proof
body_md:
The statements when $Y = X^0$ are based on the following well-known probability fact: lf $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ and $(f_n')_{n=1}^\infty$ are two sequences of random variables, each of which is independent, and, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\mathrm{dist}(f_n) = \mathrm{dist}(f_n')$, then $\mathrm{dist}((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty) = \mathrm{dist}((f_n')_{n=1}^\infty)$. In particular, if $(Z_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ is a independent sequence of subspaces of $X^0$ and  $J_n:Z_n\to X^0$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, are distributional embeddings with independent ranges, then the operator $J:[(Z_n)_{n=1}^\infty]\to X^0$ given by
\[J\Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\Big) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty J_nf_n\]
is a distributional embedding. We will elaborate on the details of the statements for $Y=H_X$, starting with \ref{canonical properties of independent sums a}. By the second part of \Cref{independence} \ref{square function-independence} it follows that each of the sequences of spaces $(J_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty$ and $(J'_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty$ is linearly independent, and thus the map $J:\big\langle \big(J_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty\big\rangle\to \big\langle\big(J'_n(Z_n)\big)_{n=1}^\infty\big\rangle$ given by $J_nf_n \mapsto J_n'f_n$ is a linear surjection. Using both statements in \Cref{independence} \ref{square function-independence}, we get that for any eventually zero sequence $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\in\prod_{n=1}^\infty X_n$,
\begin{align*}
S\Big(J\big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_nf_n\big)\Big) &= S\Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_n'f_n\Big)  = \Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty S^2(J_n'f_n)\Big)^{1/2}\equiv^\mathrm{dist} \Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty S^2(J_nf_n)\Big)^{1/2}\\
& = S\Big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_nf_n\Big).
\end{align*}
Therefore, $J$ extends to a square function-distributional isomorphism. Statements~\ref{canonical properties of independent sums b} and~\ref{canonical properties of independent sums c} are easy applications of~\ref{canonical properties of independent sums a}, we thus prove~\ref{canonical properties of independent sums d}. We fix collections of subspaces $(Z_m^n)_{m,n=1}^\infty$ of $H_X$ and square function-distributional isomorphisms $J_m^n:Z_m^n\to H_X$ with square function-independent ranges to define
\[\big(\oplus_{m,n=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}} = \big[\big(J_m^n(Z_m^n)\big)_{m,n=1}^\infty\big].\]
We can also define, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[W_n:=\big(\oplus_{m=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}} = [(J_m^n(Z^n_m))_{m=1}^\infty].\]
Using \Cref{also applies for summable} it is straightforward to show that the spaces $(W_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ are square function-independent, and we may therefore use the identity maps $I:W_n\to H_X$ to define
\[\big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty W_n\big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}} = [(W_n)_{n=1}^\infty].\]
We have therefore shown,
\[\Big(\oplus_{n=1}^\infty\big(\oplus_{m=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{X,\mathrm{ind}}\Big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}} = [(W_n)_{n=1}^\infty] = \big[\big(J_m^n(Z_m^n)\big)_{m,n=1}^\infty\big] = \big(\oplus_{m,n=1}^\infty Z_m^n\big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}}.\]
The equality holds because of the embeddings we chose to define the independent sums.

\label{BRS definition sums}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space and $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$. We define the subspaces $R_\alpha^{Y}$, $0\leq \alpha<\omega_1$, of $Y$, by transfinite recursion.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item In the base case, we let $R_0^{Y} = \{0\}$.

\item In the successor case $\alpha = \beta+1$, we let
\[R^{Y}_\alpha = \big(R^{Y}_\beta\oplus R^{Y}_\beta\big)^+_{\mathrm{disj}}.\]

\item In the limit case we let
\[R^{Y}_\alpha = \big(\oplus_{\beta<\alpha}R^{Y}_\beta\big)_{Y,\mathrm{ind}}.\]

\end{enumerate}

\label{disjointly branching tree operations}
We define two operations for constructing disjointly branching trees.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),]

\item\label{disjointly branching tree operations a} For a disjointly branching tree $\mathcal{T}$, we define
\[\mathcal{T}^+ = \big\{\{0\}\cup\{k+1:k\in F\}:F\in\mathcal{T}\big\}\cup\{\emptyset\},\]
which is again a disjointly branching tree.

\item\label{disjointly branching tree operations b}

Let $S$ be a countable set, and let $(\mathcal{T}_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of disjointly branching trees. We define their disjoint union, which is again a disjointly branching tree, as follows. For each $s\in S$, let $\mathcal{T}_s'$ be a disjointly branching tree isomorphic to $\mathcal{T}_s$, chosen so that the sets $\cup \mathcal{T}_s'$, $s\in S$, are pairwise disjoint, and let
\[\sqcup_{s\in S}\mathcal{T}_s = \cup_{s\in S} \mathcal{T}_s'.\]
For notational simplicity, we suppress the dependence of the disjoint union on the particular choice of copies $(\mathcal{T}'_s)_{s\in S}$, which, for the most part, is immaterial (see \Cref{remark on disjoint union}~\ref{remark on disjoint union b} and \Cref{tree BRS spaces include sum BRS spaces}). 

\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $((b^k_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}})_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}$ and $((\hat b^k_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{\hat h(k)}})_{k\in\cup\mathcal{S}}$ be the systems from \Cref{simple BRS basis} associated with $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}$. For $k\in\cup \mathcal{T}$ and $m\in\cup\mathcal{S}$, let $F(k)$ and $\hat F(m)$ denote  the unique members of $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ with maxima $k$ and $m$.  Let $\phi:\cup\mathcal{T}\to\cup\mathcal{S}$ witness the isomorphism of $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ as in \Cref{what tree isomorphisms look like} \ref{what tree isomorphisms look like b}. Then, for every $k\in\cup\mathcal{T}$, $\phi(F(k)) = \hat F(\phi(k))$, and in particular,
\[h(k) = |F(k)| - 1 = |\hat F(\phi(k))| - 1 = \hat h(\phi(k)).\]
Hence, $((\hat b^k_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{\hat h(k)}})_{k\in\cup\mathcal{S}} = ((\hat b^{\phi(k)}_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}})_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}$ and the correspondence  $b^k_I\mapsto \hat b^{\phi(k)}_I$ extends to a linear bijection between the linear spans of these systems. We will next show that it is a distributional isomorphism.

Let $J:L_0(\sigma(r_k:k\in\cup\mathcal{T}))\to L_0$ denote the distributional embedding given by $r_k\mapsto r_{\phi(k)}$. It is worth noting that, since $\phi$ may fail to be globally increasing, $J$ is a priori not a square function-distributional embedding. However, for every $F\in\mathcal{T}$ and $k\in F$, the restriction $\phi|_F$ is increasing, so
\[Jr_k = r_{\phi(k)} = J_{\phi(F)}J_F^{-1}r_k.\]
Because distributional isomorphisms are homomorphisms, we deduce $J|_{Y_F} = J_{\phi(F)}J_F^{-1}|_{Y_F}$. In particular, for every $k\in\cup\mathcal{T}$ and $I\in \mathcal{D}_{h(k)}$,
\[Jb_I^k = J_{\hat F(\phi(k))}J_{F(k)}^{-1}b_I^k = \hat b_I^{\phi(k)},\]
and thus, $b^k_I\mapsto \hat b^{\phi(k)}_I$ extends to a distributional embedding. To conclude, we will show that it extends to a square function-distributional isomorphism as well.

Let us fix a collection of scalars $((a^k_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}})_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}$, with only finitely many non-zero terms and let $f = \sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k b_I^k$. Recall that $J$ is a homomorphism and, by the proof of \Cref{standard square function distributional isomorphism}, for every $F\in\mathcal{T}$, $SJ_F = \tilde J_FS$:
\begin{align*}
S(Jf) &= \Big(\sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}S^2\big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k \hat b_I^{\phi(k)}\big)\Big)^{1/2} = \Big(\sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}S^2\big(J_{F(k)}\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k b_I^{k}\big)\Big)^{1/2}\\
&= \Big(\sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}\tilde J_{F(k)}S^2\big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k b_I^{k}\big)\Big)^{1/2} = \Big(\sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}\tilde JS^2\big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k b_I^{k}\big)\Big)^{1/2}\\
&=\tilde J\Big(\sum_{k\in\cup\mathcal{T}}S^2\big(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{D}^{h(k)}}a_I^k b_I^{k}\big)\Big)^{1/2} = \tilde JS(f),
\end{align*}
which yields $\mathrm{dist}(S(Jf)) = \mathrm{dist}(S(f))$.

Let $X$ be a Haar system space, $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$, and $\mathcal{T}$ be a disjointly branching tree. Then $R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$ is complemented in $Y$ if and only if $P_\mathcal{T}$ extends to a bounded linear operator on $Y$. title: Proof
body_md:
This proof is more naturally stated in the context of the measure space $\{-1,1\}^\mathbb{N}$, instead of $[0,1]$. Nevertheless, we use the language of the latter for consistency. We focus on the case $Y = H_X$, because the case $Y = X^0$ is nearly identical. Assume that $Q:Y\to Y$ is an arbitrary bounded linear projection onto $R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$.

Let $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and let $T_k:\langle\{h_I:I\in\mathcal{D}\}\rangle \to \langle\{h_I:I\in\mathcal{D}\}\rangle$ denote the linear operator such that, for every $I\in\mathcal{D}^k$, $Tf$ swaps $f|_{I^+}$ with $f|_{I^-}$. Then $T_k$ is an onto distributional isomorphism with $T_k^2 = id$. Note that, for $k,k'\in\mathbb{N}_0$, $T_kT_{k'} = T_{k'}T_k$ and  furthermore, for every finite $F\subset\mathbb{N}_0$, $\mathbb{E}_FT_k = T_k\mathbb{E}_F$. Combined with $T_k$  being a distributional isomorphism, this implies that $T_k$ is a square function-distributional embedding and thus extends to an onto isometry $T_k:Y\to Y$. For every finite $A\subset\mathbb{N}_0$ we define the operator $T_A = \prod_{k\in A}T_k$. Note that, for any finite $A,B\subset \mathbb{N}_0$, $T_AT_B = T_{A\triangle B}$, and in particular $T_A^2 = id$.

For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let
\[P_n = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{A\subset\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}T_AQT_A.\]
Noting that, for all finite $A\subset\mathbb{N}_0$, $R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$ is $T_A$-invariant, we obtain that $P_n$ is a bounded linear projection onto $R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$ of norm at most $\|Q\|$. It can be shown that for every $I\in\mathcal{D}$, $(P_nh_I)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is Cauchy (this is based on the set $\{T_Ah_I:A\in[\mathbb{N}_0]^{<\infty}\}$  being finite and $T_A\mathbb{E}_m = T_{A\cap \{0,\ldots,m\}}\mathbb{E}_m$), and therefore $(P_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in the strong operator topology to a bounded linear projection  $P:Y\to R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$, with $\|P\|\leq \|Q\|$. For a finite non-empty $A\subset\mathbb{N}_0$, consider the Walsh function $w_A = \prod_{k\in A}r_k$. We will show that, for every such $A$, $w_A$ is an eigenvector of $P$ (with eigenvalue $\lambda_A = 0$ or $1$, because $P$ is a projection). Because the Walsh functions are an orthonormal basis of $L_2^0$ (and their linear span is dense in $Y$), this suggests that $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto the closed linear span of $\{w_A:\lambda_A = 1\}$ (which coincides with $[\{w_A:\emptyset\neq A\subset F, F\in\mathcal{T}\}] = R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}$).

By approximation, it suffices to show that, for a finite non-empty $B\subset\mathbb{N}_0$ and fixed $\max(B)\leq m<n\in\mathbb{N}$,  the Walsh function $w_B$ and is an eigenvector of $P_{m,n} = \mathbb{E}_mP_n\mathbb{E}_m$. The Walsh functions $w_A$, $\emptyset\neq A\subset\{0,\ldots,m\}$, form an orthonormal basis of $\langle\{h_I:I\in\mathcal{D}_{m-1}\}\rangle$. Expand
\begin{align}
\label{BRS orthocomplemented or not at all eq1}
P_{m,n}w_B = \sum_{\emptyset\neq A\subset\{0,\ldots,m\}}\lambda_Aw_A,
\end{align}
for some unique collection of coefficients $\lambda_A$, $\emptyset\neq A\subset\{0,\ldots,m\}$. For a fixed, but arbitrary, $k\leq m$, note that $T_kP_{m,n} = P_{m,n}T_k$ and, for $\emptyset\neq A\subset\{0,\ldots,m\}$, $T_kw_A = (-1)^{\delta_k(A)}w_A$. Applying $T_k$ to both sides of \eqref{BRS orthocomplemented or not at all eq1}, we obtain
\[P_{m,n}w_B = \sum_{\emptyset\neq A\subset\{0,\ldots,m\}}\lambda_A(-1)^{\delta_k(A)-\delta_k(B)}w_A.\]
By the uniqueness of the coefficients, $\lambda_A\neq 0$ implies $\delta_k(A) = \delta_k(B)$. Because $k\leq m$ was arbitrary, $A = B\cap \{0,\ldots,m\} =B$. In conclusion, $P_{m,n}w_B = \lambda_{B}w_{B}$.

label: tree detecting complemented copy definition
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space, $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$, and $W$ be a Banach space. For $C\geq 1$, we define $\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ as the collection of all finite sequences
\[\big((T_0,P_0),\ldots,(T_n,P_n)\big)\]
satisfying the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition a} For $0\leq k\leq n$, $T_k:Y_k\to W$ is a linear operator such that, for all $f\in Y_k$,
\[C^{-1}\|f\|\leq \|T_kf\| \leq C\|f\|.\]

\item\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition b} For $1\leq k\leq n$, $T_k|_{Y_{k-1}} = T_{k-1}$.

\item\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition c} For $0\leq k\leq n$, $P_k:W\to W$ is a projection onto $T_k(Y_k)$ of norm at most $C$.

\item\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition d} For all $0\leq k,m\leq n$, $P_kP_m = P_{k\wedge m}$.

\item\label{tree detecting complemented copy definition e} For $1\leq k\leq n$, $P_{k-1}T_k = T_{k-1}\mathbb{E}_{k-1}|_{Y_k}$.

\end{enumerate}

title: Notation
body_md:
The collection $\mathscr{T}=\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ in \Cref{tree detecting complemented copy definition} is a tree under the partial order of initial segments. Following \cite{bourgain:1980}, let $\mathscr{T}^{(0)}=\mathscr{T}$, given $\alpha$, let $\mathscr{T}^{(\alpha+1)}$ be the set of all non-maximal elements of $\mathscr{T}^{(\alpha)}$, and for a limit ordinal $\alpha$, set
\[\mathscr{T}^{(\alpha)}=\bigcap_{\beta<\alpha}\mathscr{T}^{(\beta)}.\]
If $\mathscr{T}$ is well-founded, meaning it contains no infinite chains, this transfinite derivation exhausts $\mathscr{T}$ at some ordinal stage. The least such ordinal is a successor ordinal, and its predecessor is called the order of $\mathscr{T}$, denoted by $o[\mathscr{T}]$, i.e.,
\[o[\mathscr{T}]=\min\bigl\{\alpha:\mathscr{T}^{(\alpha)}=\{ \emptyset \}\bigr\}.\]
If $\mathscr{T}$ is not well-founded, it is called ill-founded.

title: Remark
body_md: If we had not allowed the empty sequence in $\mathscr{T}$, we would define $o[\mathscr{T}]=\min\bigl\{\alpha:\mathscr{T}^{(\alpha)}= \emptyset \bigr\}$ as in~\cite{bourgain:1980} to compensate for a shift by one. These changes do not affect whether $\mathscr{T}$ is well-founded; hence, \cite[Proposition~3]{bourgain:1980}, which will play an important role in the next proof, remains valid in our setting.

label: well-founded iff countable ordinal
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{well-founded iff countable ordinal}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space, $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$, $W$ be a separable Banach space, and $C\geq 1$. If $\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ is well-founded, then $o[\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)] <\omega_1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For a fixed $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, consider the space $\mathcal{L}(Y_k,W) = \{T:Y_k\to W\text{ linear and bounded}\}$, equipped with the norm topology, and the set $B_{\mathcal{L}(W)} = \{T:W\to W\text{ linear and }\|T\|\leq 1\}$, equipped with the strong operator topology. Since $Y_k$ is finite-dimensional and $W$ is separable, both spaces are Polish, and thus, so is their product
\[S_k =  \mathcal{L}(Y_k,W) \times CB_{\mathcal{L}(W)}.\]
By \cite[Proposition 3]{bourgain:1980}, it suffices to show that, for an arbitrary fixed $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, the set $\mathscr{T}_n$ consisting of all $\big((T_0,P_0),\ldots,(T_n,P_n)\big)\in\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ is closed in the product space $\prod_{k=0}^n S_k$. Recalling that composition is jointly continuous in the strong operator topology on bounded sets, it follows readily that if $\big((T^i_0,P^i_0),\ldots,(T^i_n,P^i_n)\big)_{i=1}^\infty$ in $\mathscr{T}_n$ converges to $\big((T_0,P_0),\ldots,(T_n,P_n)\big)$, then the limit also belongs to $\mathscr{T}_n$.

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Fatou property definition}
We say that a Haar system space $X$ satisfies the Fatou property if whenever $(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is a bounded sequence in $X$ and $0\le f_n \uparrow f$ almost everywhere for some $f\in L_0$, then $f\in X$ and $\|f_n\|_X\uparrow \|f\|_X$.

label: Doob's and Hardy analogue
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Doob's and Hardy analogue}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space satisfying Fatou's property.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item  If $(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is a supermartingale in $X$ with $\sup_n \|f_n\|_X < \infty$, then it converges almost everywhere to a function $f\in X$, and $\|f\|_X\le \liminf_n \|f_n\|_X$.

\item The Haar system is a boundedly complete basis for $H_X$.

\end{enumerate}
In particular, if $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$ and $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ is a dyadic martingale bounded with respect to $Y$, then it converges almost everywhere to an $f\in Y$, and $\|f\|_Y\le \liminf_n \|f_n\|_Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Doob's convergence theorem for supermartingales bounded in $L_1$, the sequence $(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ converges almost everywhere to a function $f\in L_1$. Now we apply \cite[Chapter~1, Lemma~1.15~(ii)]{bennett:sharpley:1988} (where Banach function spaces are assumed, by definition, to satisfy the Fatou property), i.e., Fatou's lemma in $X$, to conclude that $f\in X$ and $\|f\|_X \le \liminf_n \|f_n\|_X$.

Enumerate $\mathcal{D}$ lexicographically as $I_1<I_2<\cdots$, and let $(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be scalars such that, letting $f_n = \sum_{k=1}^na_kh_{I_k}$, $\sup\|f_n\|_{H_X}<\infty$. Then, $(S(f_n))_{n=1}^\infty$ is a bounded and increasing sequence in $X$. Because $X$ satisfies Fatou's property, its limit, call it $g$, is in $X$. Because $\|\cdot\|_X\not\asymp\|\cdot\|_\infty$, by \cite[Proposition 2.4.7]{speckhofer:2025:thesis}, $\lim_n\|S(f_n)-g\|_X=0$. By the same argument, for every $m\in\mathbb{N}$, the increasing limit of $(S(f_n-f_m))_{n=1}^\infty$, namely $\sqrt{g^2 - S^2(f_m)}$, is in $X$ and $\lim_n\|S(f_n-f_m) - \sqrt{g^2 - S^2(f_m)}\|_X = 0$. Similarly, $\lim_m\|\sqrt{g^2 - S^2(f_m)}\|_X = 0$. In conclusion, $\lim_m\lim_n\|S(f_n-f_m)\|_X = 0$, i.e., $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ is Cauchy in $H_X$.

label: index main theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{index main theorem}
Let $X$ be a Haar system space  and let $Y = X^0$ or $H_X$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\item\label{index main theorem a} If a separable Banach space $W$ contains a complemented copy of a Banach space $V$ then
\[i_Y[V]\leq i_Y[W].\]

\item\label{index main theorem b} If $X$ satisfies the Fatou property then a separable Banach space $W$ contains a complemented copy of $Y$ if and only if
\[i_Y[W] = \omega_1.\]

\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is straightforward, and we omit the proof. By \Cref{rem:index-omega1-ill-founded}, the second assertion is equivalent to the ill-foundedness of $\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ for some $C\ge 1$.

Assume there exist an isomorphic embedding $T:Y\to W$ and a bounded linear projection $P:W\to W$ onto $T[Y]$. For $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$ define $T_k=T|_{Y_k}$ and $P_k=T\mathbb{E}_kT^{-1}P$. Then $(T_k,P_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ forms an infinite chain in $\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ with $C=\|T\|\|T^{-1}\|\|P\|$.

Conversely, let $C\ge 1$ and suppose $\mathscr{T}(Y,W,C)$ contains an infinite chain $(T_k,P_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$. By \Cref{tree detecting complemented copy definition} \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition b}, the operators $T_k$ extend each other on domains whose union is dense in $Y$, and by \Cref{tree detecting complemented copy definition} \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition a}, they define an isomorphic embedding $T:Y\to W$.

We construct a bounded projection $P:W\to W$ onto $T(Y)$. For $w\in W$ set $f_k=T_k^{-1}P_kw$. By \Cref{tree detecting complemented copy definition} \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition d} and \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition e}, $\mathbb{E}_k f_{k+1}=f_k$, $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, which is immediate upon rewriting \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition e} as $T_{k-1}^{-1}P_{k-1}T_k=\mathbb{E}_{k-1}|_{Y_k}$. Thus $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is a bounded dyadic martingale, and by \Cref{Doob's and Hardy analogue}, there exists $f\in Y$ such that $f_k\to f$ almost everywhere and $\|f\|_Y\leq C^2\|w\|$. Define $Pw=Tf$. Then $P:W\to W$ is a linear projection onto $T(Y)$ of norm at most $C^3$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We define an order-preserving injection from $\mathcal{T}$ into $\mathscr{T}(Y,R_\mathcal{T}^{Y},1)$ as follows. Let $\emptyset\mapsto \emptyset$, and for $F=\{k_0<\cdots<k_n\}\in\mathcal{T}$, set
\[F \mapsto \big((T_0^F,P_0^F),\ldots,(T_n^F,P_n^F)\big),\]
where for $0\le m\le n$,
\begin{align*}
T_m^F &= J_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}}:Y_m\to Y_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}}\subset R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}\text{ and }\\
P_m^F &= \mathbb{E}_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}}:R_\mathcal{T}^{Y}\to Y_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}}.
\end{align*}

By \Cref{norm-one projection and isometry}, each $T_m^F$ is an isometry and each $P_m^F$ is a norm-one projection. Verification of \Cref{tree detecting complemented copy definition}~\ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition a}--\ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition e} is routine. For instance, condition \ref{tree detecting complemented copy definition e} reduces, for $1\le m\le n$, to
\[\mathbb{E}_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_{m-1}\}} J_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}}=J_{\{k_0,\ldots,k_m\}} \mathbb{E}_{m-1}|_{Y_m},\]
which is immediate on $(h_I)_{I\in\mathcal{D}_m}$.

The ``in particular'' statement follows from the fact that $R_\alpha^{Y}$ is isometric to $R_{\mathcal{T}_\alpha}^{Y}$ (see \Cref{tree BRS spaces include sum BRS spaces}), together with \Cref{rem:order-of-ordinal-trees}.

label: dfn:faithful-HS
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{dfn:faithful-HS}
  For every $I\in \mathcal{D}$, let $\mathcal{B}_I$ be a finite subcollection of $\mathcal{D}$. Moreover, let $(\theta_K)_{K\in \mathcal{D}}\in \{ \pm 1 \}^{\mathcal{D}}$ be a family of signs, and let $(\eta_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ be a family of positive numbers with $0\le \eta_I < 1$ for all $I$. For $I\in \mathcal{D}$, put $\tilde{h}_I = \sum_{K\in \mathcal{B}_I} \theta_Kh_K$. We say that $(\tilde{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ is an $(\eta_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$-faithful Haar system if the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),]
    \item\label{cond:faithful-i-copy} For every $I\in \mathcal{D}$, the collection $\mathcal{B}_I$ consists of pairwise disjoint dyadic intervals, and $\mathcal{B}_I\cap \mathcal{B}_J = \emptyset$ for all $I\ne J\in \mathcal{D}$.
    \item\label{cond:faithful-ii-copy} For every $I\in \mathcal{D}$, we have $\mathcal{B}_{I^{\pm }}^{*}\subset [\tilde{h}_I = \pm 1]$ and $|\mathcal{B}_{I^{\pm }}^{*}|\ge (1-\eta_I) \cdot \tfrac12 |\mathcal{B}_I^{*}|$.
  \end{enumerate}
  If $\eta_I = 0$ for all $I\in \mathcal{D}$, we call $(\tilde{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ a faithful Haar system.

title: Proof
body_md:
This is proved in \cite[Theorem~7.3]{lechner:speckhofer:2025} (see also \cite[Theorem 3.5.3]{speckhofer:2025:thesis} for more details). In our main results, the most important case is $Y = X^0$, where $X$ is a Haar system space in which the Haar system is unconditional. In this case, the proof is much shorter, and we have chosen to include it for convenience.

  First, we assume that $(\tilde{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ is a faithful Haar system.
  Then $B$ is a distributional isomorphism on $\langle\{ \chi_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \}  \rangle$ and hence an isometry on~$X^0$.
  We can extend the operators $B$ and~$A$ from $\langle \{ h_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \} \rangle$ to $\langle \{ \chi_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \} \rangle$ as follows: For $\alpha\in \mathbb{R}$, $x_0\in \langle \{ h_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \} \rangle$, and $x = \alpha \chi_{[0,1)} + x_0$, we put $\bar{B}x = \alpha \chi_{[0,1)} + Bx_0$ and $\bar{A}x = \alpha \chi_{[0,1)} + Ax_0$. Then the boundedness of $\bar{A}$, and hence of $A$, follows by duality: By \Cref{pro:HS-1d}~\ref{pro:HS-1d:iii}, $\bar{B}$ is also an isometry in the $X^{*}$-norm,
  and for all $x,y\in \langle \{ \chi_{[0,1)} \}\cup  \{ h_I : I\in \mathcal{D} \} \rangle$, we have $\langle y, \bar{A}x \rangle = \langle \bar{B}y, x \rangle$.

  If $(\tilde{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ is not faithful, then we can find a faithful Haar system $(\hat{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$ with Haar supports~$\hat{\mathcal{B}}_I$ such that $\mathcal{B}_I\subset \hat{\mathcal{B}}_I$ for all $I\in \mathcal{D}$ (such a system can be constructed inductively: if $\hat{h}_{\pi(I)}$ has already been defined for some $I\in \mathcal{D}$, we extend the collection $\mathcal{B}_I$ to $\hat{\mathcal{B}}_I$ by inserting sufficiently small, disjoint dyadic intervals which precisely cover the set $[\hat{h}_{\pi(I)} = \varepsilon(I)]\setminus \mathcal{B}_I^{*}$, and which do not yet appear in any previously constructed collection; see \Cref{fig:almost-faithful-and-faithful}).
  Now let $\hat{A},\hat{B}$ denote the operators associated with $(\hat{h}_I)_{I\in \mathcal{D}}$. We already know that they are bounded. Moreover, let $\mathcal{C} = \bigcup_{I\in \mathcal{D}} \mathcal{B}_I$, and let $R$ denote the Haar multiplier defined by $R h_K = h_K$ for $K\in \mathcal{C}$ and $Rh_k = 0$ for $K\in \mathcal{D}\setminus \mathcal{C}$. Thus, $R \hat{h}_I = \tilde{h}_I$ for all $I\in \mathcal{D}$, and by unconditionality, $R$ is bounded on $X$. Now we can write $B = R \hat{B}$ and $A = M \hat{A} R$, where $M$ is the linear extension of
  \begin{equation*}
    Mh_I = \frac{|I|}{|\mathcal{B}_I^{*}|} h_I,\qquad I\in \mathcal{D}.
  \end{equation*}
  Hence, it only remains to prove that $\sup_{I\in \mathcal{D}} |I|/|\mathcal{B}_I^{*}| < \infty$.
  This follows by repeatedly applying \Cref{dfn:faithful-HS}~\ref{cond:faithful-ii-copy}: For $I\in \mathcal{D}$ with $|I| = 2^{-n}$, we have
  \begin{equation*}
    |\mathcal{B}_I^{*}| \ge \Bigl( \prod_{J\in \mathcal{D}: J\supsetneq I} (1-\eta_J) \Bigr) \frac{|\mathcal{B}_{[0,1)}^{*}|}{2^n}
    \ge \Bigl( 1 - \sum_{J\in \mathcal{D}: J\supsetneq I} \eta_J \Bigr) \frac{|\mathcal{B}_{[0,1)}^{*}|}{2^n} \ge (1-\sigma) |\mathcal{B}_{[0,1)}^{*}| |I|.
  \end{equation*}
  Thus, $A$ and $B$ extend to bounded linear operators on $X^0$, given by the two norm-convergent series in~\eqref{eq:9}.

label: thm:alternatives-ri
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alternatives-ri}
  Let $X$ be a Haar system space with the Fatou property and non-trivial Boyd indices, and let $Y = X^0$. Then, one of the following exclusive alternatives holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),]
    \item\label{thm:alternatives:a} There exists a strictly increasing transfinite sequence of countable ordinals $(\alpha_\xi)_{\xi< \omega_1}$ such that the spaces $R_{\alpha_\xi}^{Y}$, $\xi < \omega_1$, are pairwise non-isomorphic.
    \item\label{thm:alternatives:b} For every ordinal $\omega \le \alpha < \omega_1$, the space $R_\alpha^{Y}$ is isomorphic to $Y$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Moreover,~\ref{thm:alternatives:b} is equivalent to~\ref{thm:alternatives:c} and~\ref{thm:alternatives:d} below.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),start=3]
    \item\label{thm:alternatives:c} For some $\alpha < \omega_1$, the space $R_\alpha^{Y}$ contains a complemented copy of~$Y$.
    \item\label{thm:alternatives:d} There exists an independent sequence of functions in $Y$ equivalent to the Haar system whose closed linear span is complemented in $Y$.
  \end{enumerate}

Then, one of the exclusive alternatives~\ref{thm:alternatives:a} and~\ref{thm:alternatives:b} in \Cref{thm:alternatives-ri} holds, and~\ref{thm:alternatives:b} is equivalent to~\ref{thm:alternatives:c}.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:tree-spaces-uncomplemented}
  Let $Y =L_1^0$, $H^1$, $L_{\Phi}^0$, or $H_{L_{\Phi}}$, where $\Phi$ is as in \Cref{ntt:orlicz-space} for some $0 < \alpha < 1/2$. Then the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item\label{thm:tree-spaces-uncomplemented:a} For every well-founded disjointly branching tree $\mathcal{T}$ with $o[\mathcal{T}]\geq \omega\cdot 2$, the space $R_{\mathcal{T}}^{Y}$ is uncomplemented in $Y$. In particular, this holds for the space $R_{\mathcal{T}_\alpha}^Y$ if $\omega\cdot 2 \le \alpha < \omega_1$.
    \item\label{thm:tree-spaces-uncomplemented:b} For every $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, there exist realizations of $\mathcal{T}_{\omega + n}$ for which $R_{\mathcal{T}_{\omega + n}}^Y$ is uncomplemented in~$Y$.
    \item\label{thm:tree-spaces-uncomplemented:c} For every $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, there exist realizations of $\mathcal{T}_{\omega + n}$ (such as the one in \Cref{exa:ordinal-trees}) for which $R_{\mathcal{T}_{\omega + n}}^{H^1}$ is complemented in~$H^1$.
  \end{enumerate}

title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:T-alpha-yardstick}

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The construction used in this proof is illustrated in \Cref{fig:yardstick-from-tree}.
  Recall that $\mathcal{T}_\alpha = \sqcup_{0\leq \beta<\alpha}\mathcal{T}_\beta = \cup_{0\le \beta < \alpha} \mathcal{T}_\beta'$, where for each $\beta < \alpha$, $\mathcal{T}_\beta'$ is a disjointly branching tree isomorphic to $\mathcal{T}_\beta$, chosen so that the sets $\cup \mathcal{T}_\beta'$, $\beta < \alpha$, are pairwise disjoint. For $r = 1,\dots,m$, let $G_r$ be the unique element of $\mathcal{T}_{\omega + k + r}'$ with cardinality $k + r$. Then $G_r$ has an infinite successor set in $\mathcal{T}_{\omega + k + r}'$, as follows from the structure of $\mathcal{T}_{\omega + k + r}$. Thus, for every $r$, we can find $g_r\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $g_r > \max(G_1\cup \dots\cup G_m)$ and $F_r := G_r\cup \{ g_r \}\in \mathcal{T}_{\omega + k + r}'$. Then $F_1,\dots,F_m$ is a $k$-yardstick family in $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$.
